stem: What is price analysis?

options.text: Examining a proposed price without evaluating its separate cost elements and profit
options.why: That is the FAR definition.
That is audit work, often by DCAA.

options.text: Evaluating each cost element and the proposed profit
options.why: That is cost analysis.
That is technical evaluation.

stem: Which two price analysis techniques does the FAR treat as preferred?

options.text: Comparing the prices offered in the competition, and comparing with prior prices for the same or similar items
options.why: These two come first in the FAR's list.

options.text: Comparing with the IGCE, and asking the contractor to explain its price
options.why: These are useful but not the preferred techniques.
Useful as checks, not the preferred techniques.

options.text: Reviewing the contractor's labor rates and overhead
options.why: That is cost analysis.

stem: Adequate price competition exists when:

options.text: Two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, submit priced offers that meet the requirement, with award on best value where price is a substantial factor
options.why: Those are the conditions in FAR 15.403-2(c)(1), along with no finding that the winning price is unreasonable.

options.text: Any single offer comes in below the IGCE
options.why: One offer is not competition.
Offerors must compete independently.
Incumbency has nothing to do with it.

stem: You compare a quote with a price paid 14 months ago for the same item. What should you adjust for?

options.text: Time (inflation), quantity and differences in terms
options.why: Prior prices are only comparable after adjusting for what changed.

options.text: Nothing; the same item means the same price
options.why: Markets and quantities change.
Shipping is one difference, not the only one.
Price analysis does not break out profit.

stem: What is unbalanced pricing?

options.text: One or more line items significantly overstated or understated, even though the total price may look acceptable
options.why: Unbalanced pricing hides risk inside line items.

options.text: Any total price above the IGCE
options.why: A high total is not the same as unbalanced line items.

options.text: A price below the contractor's cost
options.why: That is a buy-in risk, a different issue.
Lateness is unrelated.

stem: On a simplified buy you receive only one quote. What does the contracting officer do?

options.text: Still determine the price is fair and reasonable, using other evidence such as catalogs, prior prices or market research, and document it
options.why: A single quote can be reasonable when other evidence supports it.
One quote does not require cancellation.

options.text: Require certified cost or pricing data
options.why: Certified data are never required at or below the SAT.
A fair and reasonable price determination is always required.

stem: A 'fair and reasonable' price is:

options.text: Fair to both the Government and the contractor
options.why: It must not be too high for the Government or too low for the contractor to perform.
A price can be too low to be realistic.
The IGCE is one benchmark, not the definition.
Catalog prices still need to be compared with the market.

stem: For a DoW prime contract awarded after 30 June 2026, certified cost or pricing data are required (unless an exception applies) when the contract is expected to exceed:

options.why: The FY2026 NDAA raised DoW's threshold; DoW applies it through the DFARS 215.403-3 class deviation.
$2.5 million is the governmentwide FAR figure and DoW's figure for earlier awards.
That is an outdated figure.
That is the SAT.

stem: Which is an exception to requiring certified cost or pricing data?

options.why: Competition, prices set by law, commercial items and waivers are the main exceptions.

options.text: The contractor is a small business
options.why: Size is not an exception.
Cost-type contracts often require certified data.
That is when data are required, not an exception.

stem: Certified cost or pricing data are never required for:

options.text: Buys at or below the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: FAR 15.403-2(a) prohibits requiring them at or below the SAT.
Large noncompetitive buys often require them.
Services are not exempt as such.
Construction is not exempt as such.

stem: A cost is allowable only if it is:

options.text: Reasonable, allocable, consistent with CAS or GAAP, consistent with the contract terms, and not limited or disallowed by the cost principles
options.why: Those are the factors in FAR 31.201-2.
Incurring a cost does not make it allowable.
DCAA advises; the contracting officer decides.
Billing a cost does not make it allowable.

stem: Which cost is unallowable under the cost principles?

options.why: FAR 31.205 makes alcohol, entertainment, bad debts and most lobbying unallowable.
Direct labor is normally allowable.
Materials are normally allowable.
Reasonable, allocable G&A is normally allowable.

stem: Cost analysis means:

options.text: Reviewing the separate cost elements and profit in a proposal
options.why: Cost analysis looks inside the price.

options.text: Comparing the prices offered in a competition
options.why: That is price analysis.

options.text: Using dollars per pound to estimate a price
options.why: That is a parametric price analysis technique.
That is market research.

stem: Cost realism analysis matters most on which contracts?

options.why: The Government pays actual costs, so unrealistic estimates lead to overruns.
The contractor carries cost risk; realism is used only in limited cases.
Micro-purchases need only a reasonable price.
Sealed bids are decided on price.

stem: Prenegotiation objectives are:

options.text: The Government's planned positions, based on its analysis, set before negotiating
options.why: Objectives come from price, cost and technical analysis.
That is the proposal.
That is the outcome, recorded in the PNM.
The IGCE is one input, not the objective itself.

stem: Which document records the results of a negotiation?

options.why: The PNM documents objectives, positions, the agreement and the reasons.
A D&F approves certain actions; it is not a negotiation record.
A J&A justifies limiting competition.
That records a competitive award decision.

stem: In negotiation, BATNA means:

options.text: The best alternative to a negotiated agreement
options.why: Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away.

options.text: The bid acceptance and tender notice
options.why: No such term.

options.text: The budget allotment for a negotiated award
options.why: Not the meaning.
Not the meaning.

stem: Clarifications are:

options.text: Limited exchanges when award without negotiations is planned, to resolve minor issues
options.why: Clarifications do not let offerors revise proposals.

options.text: Negotiations that let every offeror revise its proposal
options.why: Those are negotiations in the competitive range.
Debriefings explain the decision after the fact.
Protests are disagreements, not exchanges.

stem: The competitive range is made up of:

options.text: The most highly rated proposals, set when negotiations will be held
options.why: The contracting officer limits negotiations to the most highly rated proposals.
Proposals with no reasonable chance can be excluded.
Ratings depend on all factors, not just price.

options.text: Offerors who attended the pre-proposal conference
options.why: Attendance does not decide the competitive range.

stem: During negotiations in a competition, which is NOT allowed?

options.text: Telling an offeror another offeror's price
options.why: Revealing competitors' prices or information is prohibited.

options.text: Pointing out significant weaknesses in the offeror's proposal
options.why: That is expected in meaningful negotiations.
Questions are normal.
Final revisions close out negotiations.

stem: A good negotiator makes concessions:

options.text: In exchange for something of value, according to the plan
options.why: Trading concessions keeps the agreement balanced and defensible.

options.text: Early and freely to build trust
options.why: Free concessions weaken the Government's position.
Negotiation involves give and take.
The contracting officer leads negotiations.

stem: Which evaluation factor must be part of every source selection?

options.why: Price or cost must be evaluated in every source selection.
Past performance is usually but not always evaluated.
Orals are optional.
It is evaluated only in some acquisitions.

stem: A tradeoff source selection:

options.text: Allows award to other than the lowest price when the better offer is worth the extra cost
options.why: Tradeoffs weigh price against non-price factors.

options.text: Always awards to the lowest price
options.why: That is LPTA.
Technical factors are central to tradeoffs.
Tradeoff is widely used in DoW.

stem: Under lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA):

options.text: Award goes to the lowest priced offer that meets all requirements, with no tradeoffs
options.why: LPTA rates proposals acceptable or unacceptable, then picks the lowest acceptable price.

options.text: The best technical proposal wins at any price
options.why: That is not LPTA.

options.text: Past performance can never be considered
options.why: Past performance can be an acceptability factor.
Discussions are possible in LPTA.

stem: Proposals must be evaluated:

options.text: Only on the factors and subfactors stated in the solicitation
options.why: Using unstated criteria is a leading cause of sustained protests.

options.text: On any factor the SSA decides is relevant
options.why: The SSA is bound by the stated criteria.

options.text: On news stories about the offerors
options.why: Outside information must be handled carefully and tied to stated factors.

options.text: Mainly on experience with the incumbent
options.why: Incumbency is not an evaluation factor.

stem: The source selection authority's decision must:

options.text: Reflect the SSA's own judgment from comparing proposals against the criteria, and document any tradeoff rationale
options.why: RFO FAR 15.205 requires independent, documented judgment.

options.text: Simply adopt the evaluation board's recommendation
options.why: The SSA may use the analysis but must decide independently.

options.text: Be given orally to save time
options.why: The decision must be documented.

options.text: Stay secret from the contracting officer
options.why: The contracting officer is the focal point and keeps the file.

stem: Before any award, the contracting officer must make:

options.text: An affirmative determination that the prospective contractor is responsible
options.why: No award without a responsibility determination.

options.text: A determination that the contractor is a small business
options.why: Size matters only for set-asides.
CPARS evaluates performance on existing contracts.
Audits are not required for every award.

stem: A contractor is listed as excluded in SAM. Can it receive a new award?

options.text: Generally no, unless the agency head finds a compelling reason
options.why: Excluded contractors may not receive new awards absent a compelling-reason determination.

options.text: Yes, if it has the lowest price
options.why: Price does not overcome an exclusion.

options.text: Yes, if it is a small business
options.why: Size does not overcome an exclusion.
Exclusions apply at every dollar level.

stem: To get a postaward debriefing, an offeror must ask in writing within:

options.text: 3 days after receiving the award notice
options.why: RFO FAR 15.301-1 keys the request window to the award notice.
Ten days is a protest timeline.
The request window is 3 days.
Far too late.

stem: After a timely request, the agency should hold the postaward debriefing:

options.text: Within 5 days of the request, to the maximum extent practicable
options.why: That is the FAR standard.
The target is 5 days.

options.text: Only after any protest is decided
options.why: Debriefings come before protests.
The 5-day target applies.

stem: A debriefing must NOT include:

options.text: Point-by-point comparisons with other offerors' proposals or their confidential information
options.why: Debriefings explain the decision without exposing competitors' proposals.

options.text: The overall evaluated price of the winning offer
options.why: That is normally included.

options.text: The debriefed offeror's significant weaknesses or deficiencies
options.why: That is a core part of a debriefing.

options.text: A summary of the rationale for award
options.why: That is included.

stem: Unsuccessful offerors in the competitive range must get an award notice within:

options.why: RFO FAR 15.207-2 requires notice within 3 days.
The requirement is 3 days.
The requirement is 3 days.
Notice is required whether or not they ask.

stem: Where are contract awards reported now that FPDS.gov has been retired?

options.why: Contract award reporting moved into SAM.gov.
CPARS holds performance evaluations.
WAWF holds invoices and receiving reports.
GFEBS is the Army's financial system.

stem: Which item is normally part of a postaward debriefing?

options.text: The overall evaluated price and technical rating of the winner and of the debriefed offeror
options.why: Debriefings share these overall results.

options.text: A copy of the winner's technical proposal
options.why: Other offerors' proposals are not released.

options.text: The names of the evaluators and their scoring sheets
options.why: Evaluator identities and individual scores are protected.
The IGCE is not shared.

stem: An offeror excluded from the competitive range wants an explanation before award. It may:

options.text: Request a preaward debriefing in writing within 3 days of receiving the exclusion notice
options.why: RFO FAR 15.206-2 covers preaward debriefings.
A preaward debriefing is available on timely request.
The window is 3 days.
It can be requested before award.

stem: A protest about a problem that is apparent in the solicitation must be filed:

options.text: Before bid opening or the closing time for receipt of proposals
options.why: Offerors cannot wait to see if they win before objecting to the solicitation.
That rule is for other protest grounds.
That rule is for matters learned in a required debriefing.
Solicitation challenges must come before closing.

stem: Other GAO protests must generally be filed within how many days after the protester knew or should have known the basis?

options.why: GAO's general timeliness rule is 10 days.
Five days applies after a required debriefing.
Thirty days is when the agency report is due.
One hundred days is GAO's decision deadline.

stem: When a debriefing is required and requested, a protest of matters learned in it can be filed with GAO within:

options.why: This keeps protesters from filing early just to protect their rights.
Three days is the debriefing request window.

options.text: 10 days after award, no matter when the debriefing is
options.why: The debriefing exception extends the window.
Too long.

stem: GAO must decide a protest within:

options.why: GAO's statutory deadline is 100 days.
Thirty-five days is the agency-protest goal.
Thirty days is the agency report deadline.
Far longer than the rule.

stem: After award, performance must be suspended for a GAO protest if it was filed within:

options.text: 10 days after award or 5 days after a required debriefing, whichever is later
options.why: That is the automatic stay rule under CICA.
The stay window is shorter.

options.text: Any time before the contract is completed
options.why: Only timely protests trigger the stay.
The window is 10 days, or 5 after a required debriefing.

stem: Who can override the automatic stay of a GAO protest?

options.text: The head of the contracting activity, in writing, on the grounds the law allows
options.why: Overrides are reserved to the HCA level and must be justified.
The contracting officer cannot override on their own.
The COR has no such authority.
Contractors cannot override stays.

stem: For DoW, GAO hears protests of task or delivery orders valued above what amount (or orders that increase the contract's scope, period or maximum value)?

options.why: The FY2025 NDAA raised DoW's order-protest floor from $25 million to $35 million.
$10 million is the civilian agency figure.
That was DoW's figure before the FY2025 NDAA.
$7.5 million is a fair-opportunity procedures tier, not a protest floor.
